title: Still giving
hook: a commentary story: when Anathapindika grows poor, he still gives what he can
carry: even a plain gift bears good fruit

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jetavana: Anathapindika laid gold across a prince's grove to give the monks a home. Your line was covered in gold. What did you give? Today, the same man with very little left. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

Broken rice and sour gruel. That's the answer Anathapindika gives when the Buddha asks him a simple question in a short discourse of the Anguttara. Are gifts still given in your household? Yes, he says. But they're coarse now. Broken rice, with sour gruel to go with it. The commentary sets this talk at a time when his fortune had slipped away. The man who once spread gold across a grove is serving what's left at the bottom of the pot. And he's still serving it. Today, what the Buddha says back.
screen: `BROKEN RICE AND SOUR GRUEL.` → `ARE GIFTS STILL GIVEN?` → `YES, BUT COARSE.`

segments.voice: First, the reply. The Buddha says that whether a gift is coarse or fine, what matters is how it's given. He names the ways: with respect, with care, with your own hand, not like tossing out scraps, and trusting that it bears fruit. Given like that, the discourse says, even a plain gift bears good fruit. Second, a story inside the story. The Buddha tells of a brahmin named Velama, long ago, who gave enormous gifts: bowls heaped with gold and silver, elephants, chariots, fine cloth. Then he says: I was Velama. But no one worthy was there to receive those gifts. Third, the ladder. So the Buddha climbs, step by step. Better than all of Velama's wealth is feeding one person of right view. Further up, building a dwelling for the sangha of the four directions, which is exactly what Anathapindika had once done. Higher still, going for refuge with a trusting heart, then keeping the precepts, then loving-kindness held even for as long as it takes to pull a cow's udder. And at the top, seeing impermanence even for the length of a finger snap. And the highest steps cost nothing at all. Fourth, the gate. A later commentary story tells of a spirit living at his gate who urged him to stop giving, now that he was poor. Anathapindika refused, and sent the spirit away. Rich or poor, he kept the door open. Still giving.
screen: `HOW IT'S GIVEN.` · `I WAS VELAMA.` · `THE LADDER OF GIFTS.` · `THE SPIRIT AT THE GATE.` · then, large: `STILL GIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give from little. Settle, and breathe. Choose something you don't have much of today. Time, maybe, or patience, or a few dollars, or energy at the end of a long week. Now find the smallest real gift you could make from it. A short call. A kind reply instead of a curt one. Half a sandwich. Then plan it with the Buddha's list: with respect, with your own hand, not like tossing out scraps. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Still giving. Grown poor, Anathapindika keeps offering coarse rice, and the Buddha says the way a gift is given is what counts. Today's word.
Your line: even a plain gift bears good fruit. Today, make your small gift with your own hand and a little care, however little it is. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana, giving, in small daily ways as well as large ones: a spoonful of rice into a monk's bowl on the alms round, flowers at a shrine, or food shared with a neighbor.

fork.setup: you're Anathapindika, poor now, and the Buddha asks whether gifts are still given in your house. what do you say?
options: no, not since the money went.
yes, but only coarse food now.
fork.reveal: he says yes, but coarse: broken rice and sour gruel. the Buddha answers that how a gift is given matters more than how fine it is.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity, and the gift itself.

trapdoor: what you thought: generosity is for people with plenty.
what it means: a poor man keeps giving coarse food, and the Buddha says a plain gift, given with respect, bears good fruit.
what a scholar hears: AN 9.20 itself doesn't say he was poor; the commentary sets it then, and the ladder ends not with any gift at all but with a moment's insight.
recall: foremost among nuns in psychic power

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verses 119–120 (Anathapindika and the spirit at the gate)

notes: AN 9.20 paraphrased. Confirm: the question 'are gifts still given in your family?'; the answer 'coarse, broken rice with sour gruel'; the ways of giving well (respectfully, thoughtfully, with one's own hand, not as discards, with a view that something will come); Velama's gifts and 'I was the brahmin Velama'; the order of the ladder (one person accomplished in view ... a dwelling for the sangha of the four quarters ... refuge ... precepts ... loving-kindness for the time of pulling a cow's udder ... perception of impermanence for a finger snap). The intermediate rungs and the numbers of Velama's gifts are deliberately omitted.
That the conversation took place when Anathapindika had grown poor is the commentary's setting, stated as such.
Spirit (devata) at the gate who tells him to stop giving and is expelled: Dhammapada commentary on verses 119–120; confirm attribution. The count of gates is omitted.
Editor: cut 'the poorest man can climb every step' (the middle rungs, like building a dwelling, need wealth); replaced with 'the highest steps cost nothing at all', which the ladder supports.
